title: Can Opus 5.5 Free us from P2W MMOs?
author: roorood
selftext:
Two weeks ago, I decided I’d had enough of every bloody MMO being ruined by P2W. It’s the only genre of games I really like, so I thought… perhaps AI is good enough now that I could use it to build my own, eventually find a way to cover the running costs, and have people enjoy it with me.

The video shows where I’m at right now, after two weeks of figuring things out. I’m a web developer by day, so game design is not my forte. But I have a bit of the ’tism, and I hyperfocus on things I want. AI really does seem able to get me past all of my knowledge gaps so far and help me produce something that excites me.

I understand it’s not much to look at right now, and it does look pretty familiar to an MMO from the past… my favorite, which went way down the P2W path. But everything you see (aside from those Brutes) was made by me (and Opus…) with no prior game development experience, in two weeks. I have a plan for a full game: a world where people like me can spend our days doing meaningful stuff without ever having to deal with P2W.

I don’t see the AAA companies ever truly moving away from sneaky cash shops, loot boxes and battle passes, so I have plenty of time to see this through. I hope to share a better, more fleshed-out and polished update in the future.

Any feedback would be great, although if it's just to shit on the quality it really doesn't need to be said.. I know... 

Cheers, Roo.

comments.author: Valdaraak
comments.body:
Opus 5.5 can free you from whatever you want to be free from. I've replaced apps on my phone with Artifacts. I've replaced that annoying ass Youtube home page and constantly changing layout with my own frontend.

I've made plenty of proof of concept games in various genres using solely Opus with no outside assets or MCP. It's at a point where just prompting can get you a game that plays well. Looks are a different story, depending on style.

Just note that the larger and more complex your project gets, the more important documentation is going to be because it's going to eat up more and more of your context window and usage to do simple things because of how much it has to read each time. And multiplayer will be its own beast to deal with.

Yours looks pretty good at the moment for being entirely Opus. I value gameplay over graphics any day.

replies.author: roorood
replies.body:
I really do believe you are right. It is incredibly liberating to have this kind of creative freedom on demand. 

If you can think it.. explain it and manage it.. AI can make it.

For my game documentation was a big thing from the go. I have a growing google drive filling up with all the documentation broken into sections of interconnected relevance. 

And from the start I’ve had Opus build everything knowing this would be a multiplayer game… that anything authoritative had to be server side.. that anything that could effect the market system we are building had to be accounted for and guarded against. 

I won’t know if I’m doing it correctly until I get to a stage where I feel ready to have others jump in and try and break it. If the way I’m using UE is optimal for performance - my threshold is 12-17ms. Anything I introduce above this is rejected and flagged for immediate optimisation.

But I’d like to think I’m going about it the right way and one day will be able to enjoy it with people who value the effort…

replies.author: Valdaraak
replies.body:
> I really do believe you are right. It is incredibly liberating to have this kind of creative freedom on demand.
> 
> If you can think it.. explain it and manage it.. AI can make it.

Correct. I've been annoyed that there hasn't been a Bloody Roar game in over 20 years. [So I'm making my own](https://i.imgur.com/KgYNeuV.png), intentionally with PS1 era styling (this is *extremely* early. It's also impressive that it's running in browser and everything you see is generated at runtime. There's no meshes or texture files, it's all math in the script files).

I'm also a big fan of old ass Unreal Tournament 99/GOTY. [So I'm making one of those too](https://i.imgur.com/op8Z1HA.jpeg), purposely styling it after the original. Again, that's running in the browser and generated at runtime. The entire game is 2 MB at the moment and has two maps with music.

And neither of those *look* that good at the moment (I've only been working on them for a few days), but they *play* very well. The shooter legit feels like I'm playing Unreal Tournament.

For MMO stuff, I'd definitely have Opus go out and do a bunch of research on MMO design and build up a reference guide. Some of them do some pretty ingenious things to keep load and latency down, others pick and choose what sits server side. For example, some unimportant monsters or NPCs might have their position client side while bosses and important NPCs like vendors will have position set and managed on the server so they're in the same spot for everyone.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Up until 500 hours in you try to do a stress test and find everything falls to shit because it didn't consider certain necessary infrastructure foundations.

Unfortunately the larger the project, the more that can go wrong. Make sure while engaging in this endeavor you constantly push it to consider:

1. Multiplayer interactions. Syncing necessary states. Delivering and receiving packets efficiently. Ideally offloading as much of the game logic as possible to clients.

2. Constantly looking for and monitoring security loopholes like spoofing packets or if you're calculating data on their PC in a way that they can intercept and edit. This is not something easily done half way through your project. Not because  the AI is incapable, but because it'll set off all kinds of security warnings for Claude/Codex and get your account flagged 7 out of 10 times even though it's a perfectly safe and reasonable use.

3. Extensibility and tech debt. MMOs are driven by their updates and evolutions. You don't want to push yourself into a corner. Updates are also a lot more difficult because pushing them out can mean breaking existing data for many players. It's not like a single player where a player can just sit and finish out their game/save on the old world before updating to try something new. If your systems aren't simple to add to without breaking old stuff, it will become a problem. AI is not generally looking out for this on its own, you have to either be outlining detailed extensible frameworks for it to then implement or try and get it to figure those out on its own. Or you can just call this one a trial to learn from, make note of all the issues you run into, then go build v2 of the mmo later with more experience. Then do the same for that one. But your players may or may not be on board with that, compared to a single player game where you can Undertale your way to success and it doesn't matter that the game is a giant ball of tangled spaghetti because it plays fine and completes and then you go into #2 with a fresh slate and no one cares because it all worked out.

replies.author: Valdaraak
replies.body:
> Extensibility and tech debt.

Adding to this, every MMO has tech debt and it always ends up being an annoying thorn that they can't get rid of and have to constantly work around. Content never goes away in MMOs. Errors and spaghetti code from early dev will bite you a decade and multiple expansions later, without any easy way to fix it because changing the problem code will impact a dozen other systems, which will then need edits as well.
